title: The Judge and the Grain of Salt
summary: Two traders claim the same sack of salt, and a highland judge settles the matter with nothing but a cup of clean water.
moral: Truth dissolves slowly, but it always leaves a taste.
attribution: A traditional Amhara tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: Salt blocks and a shallow cup on a highland terrace beneath a wide sun and layered ridges

sentences.text: Two traders came before the judge of the district, each leading a donkey, each claiming the same sack of salt.
“I bought it at the market,” said the first.
“He stole it from my load while I slept,” said the second.
“I bought it,” said the first again, louder.
The judge was old and had heard a great many loud men.
He asked each of them the same questions: where they had bought the salt, what they had paid, which road they had taken.
Their answers were almost alike.
The first, however, was a man who could not stop describing his own cleverness, and the second was a man who said very little.
The judge ordered the sack untied and a handful of salt taken from the top.
He called for a cup of clean water and dropped the salt into it.
Then he asked each trader to bring his own small stock of salt, the salt he sold every day.
The first trader brought a fine white salt, coarse as the judge’s thumb.
The second brought a greyer salt, ground finer, with a smell of the road about it.
The judge dissolved a pinch of each in two more cups, and set all three cups on the table in the sun.
“Now,” he said, “speak the truth.
One of these cups will taste like the load.
The one whose salt matches the sack is the one who has been carrying it.”
The first trader looked at the cups and grew quiet.
The second drank his cup slowly, and the judge saw him smile.
The salt had settled the matter.
The first trader paid a fine and went home ashamed, and the second went on his way with his load.
The old people say the judge never raised his voice.
He only gave the truth a little water, and it spoke for itself.
